text: What lies at the core of Leonardo's vision — how he thinks, how he draws something, how he writes about something — is this freshness, this quality of one of the greatest visual geniuses who has ever lived.

The manuscripts — these codices, these notebooks — vary enormously. Some of them have been completely rebound. They range from little pocketbooks he probably kept on his belt for taking notes, to big bound volumes. What we have is a collection of manuscripts of very different shapes and sizes.

One of the characteristics of Leonardo is that if you go into any of these manuscripts, you find that nothing is ever on just one thing. There is the theme sheet — geometry, a man in profile, drapery, tree and plants, man and horseman, engineering, clouds, hair, water, storms, mountains, tower, a decorative motif, and a recipe for hair colouring. This is an extreme example, but it is rather typical. What happens with Leonardo is that things we see as separate — he didn't see these things as separate, they all flowed into each other.

The tree merges — the branching of the tree merges with the man's drapery, which then is studied separately. And it senses some familiarity, some similarity between a bending of a branch and a bending of folding drapery. We wouldn't see that, but Leonardo does.

Leonardo's map of all his varied interests shows: painting is essential for Leonardo — it's the great expression of his understanding of nature — but it's only a small proportion of what he actually did. He is always relating things we see as different. It's that essential unity of nature which gives his work its very remarkable and characteristic quality.

The microcosm — the human body, the little world — is that in our bodies, with what were then the four elements: earth, air, fire, and water, and what is out there in nature: earth, air, fire, and water — we are a little world. Leonardo calls it a little world. If we understand nature, we understand human nature, and if we understand human nature, we understand nature.

Leonardo placed the superficial vessels of the human arm beside a drawing of the Arno river near Florence. Rivers he called venae d'acqua — veins of water, or vessels of water. In this just straight comparison, you get a sense of the microcosm: the human body with its veins of blood, and the body of the earth.
He used the term the body of the earth as a living thing. That provides the essential unity at the heart of it all.

When he was thinking about branching systems in the human body — the blood vessels to the liver — he would be thinking about all other types of branching systems. He calls the vascular system the albolo delle vene — the tree of the vessels. So it is literally a tree.

Leonardo studies the lungs with the bronchi. The tubes bifurcate — at each bifurcation, two secondary tubes have an equal cross-sectional area to the main tube, so that flow will not be turbulent. This is a law which was formulated in the 17th century. But Leonardo has done it visually. He formulates a law, which I paraphrase: at each point in the system, the cross-sectional area is constant. He's applying mathematical rules to an anatomical and organic problem — the first time anyone did this.

Then he extends this to trees. If you section the trees at that point and added up their cross-sectional area, they should be equal to the main trunk. The rule that applies to the bronchi and the lungs is exactly the same as the rule that applies to trees. Why? Because both need to transmit fluids — the tree transmits sap, the lungs transmit air.

Analogy for Leonardo is a way of arguing. For Leonardo, if you've got a tight analogy, it was proof. It was an absolute truth. He identifies a governing rule that manifests in multiple domains. He calls these not mere analogies but structural identities.

The observation of the movement of water: Observe the motion of the surface of the water, which resembles the behaviour of hair, of which one depends on the weight of the strands, the other on the line of its revolving. Thus water makes revolving eddies, one part of which depends on the impetus of the principal current and the other on the incident and reflected motions. He's not just saying it looks like hair. He's saying they have the same rule. You've got the weight of the hair, the direction of the current, the tendency of water to revolve, the tendency of some hair to revolve — put them together and you get a helix.

The glass model of the aortic valve: Leonardo says have it blown in glass — so he's trying to get the neck of the aorta done in glass to see how the currents work inside it. Morteza Gharib at Caltech built the model using modern imaging techniques and confirmed exactly what Leonardo had argued: the blood spiralled back, filling the valves. Leonardo's glass model experiment, conceived 500 years ago, was verified by modern engineering methods.

The deluge drawings at Windsor: a set of late drawings. These are hydrodynamic demonstrations — he often talks about the physics of these storms in long written accounts which describe the physics as we were describing — but they have this extraordinary expressive dynamism. In the bottom left corner of one: human beings, soldiers on horses and trees, become puny in the face of this great blast of air. The battle tents — padiglioni — are being ripped out of their supports on the ground and spiral away in the air. So there is a sense of the human playing a malign force in society, but ultimately being overwhelmed. This is what I call nature's revenge: we take nature lightly at our peril.

Leonardo was trained in the studio of Andrea Verrocchio, who is a sculptor, a painter, a jack-of-all-trades of immense quality. This brought Leonardo into contact with the great work of engineering, the Brunelleschi Dome — a dome built without centering. Leonardo made drawings from machines invented by Brunelleschi: a reversible hoist, a revolving crane. These were legendary machines.

Working with nature — first of all, water. Water is immensely important for a whole series of reasons: for drinking, for power. The Archimedean screw: a spiral shaft which, when rotated in water, causes the water to go uphill. This gives a head of water. Water was very scarce — many people didn't have running water.
Leonardo does an analysis to show that you cannot achieve perpetual motion. He writes very critically about those who pursue it. Thermodynamic limits are not negotiable.

The Canal of San Cristoforo in Milan — a pound lock — the locks we are familiar with, where the lock gates come to a point with the current. Leonardo is thinking about the state of the art of canal engineering. Milan was full of very competent water engineers and military engineers. He's contributing to a common pool of knowledge.

The Scala della Sforzesca di Vigevano: you have water high up at the top of a hill and you have to get it down non-turbulently to the bottom. If you simply let it cascade down, it causes much erosion and excavation of soil at the bottom. So the Scala steps the water down. Leonardo was much impressed by this. It is a model of working with natural force rather than fighting it.

The Arno canal project: Leonardo thought seriously about how to make a canal connecting Florence to Pisa. His great arc goes up through Prato and Pistoia. You think, what is he doing here? This is enormously long-winded. But if you look at the present motorway — the Autostrada 11 — it follows exactly that route. Leonardo working with the landscape's natural logic rather than against it.

The attempt to divert the Arno around Pisa was a fiasco. It didn't work. And one of the things that Leonardo learned from this, I think, is that water doesn't like being pushed around — that water has natural tendencies, and you're better working with water.

In the Codex Leicester he describes working with nature: if you arrange weirs further upstream to direct the river in a different direction, the damage will be repaired because the river will deposit silt at the point where it was previously eroding. This is working with nature, understanding nature and persuading nature to collaborate with us in achieving our ends. The message is: collaborate with nature. Water is powerful. Work with it rather than try to push it around.

Leonardo was much involved with military designs. He called war beastly madness, but he was fascinated by it — by the forces involved, by the chance to work on a huge scale with big forces. War, drawing war machines, becomes a form of experimentation.

His ambiguity about military matters is profound. He sees these men as animalistic. He compares them to roaring lions and shrieking horses. Yet he was fascinated by the power of military inventions. There's a deep ambiguity throughout Leonardo's work: how you work with nature, how you respect it, but also a fascination — albeit a horrified fascination — with the arts of war.

Why does Leonardo, the painter, look at the inside of the human body? The answer is, for Leonardo, you have to understand everything. If you're going to understand how a figure works, then you need to know how its vascular system works, how its nervous system works. It's a totality of knowledge.

Raphael would say: Why on earth do you need to do the nerves? What's this about? But Leonardo needs to understand everything. Whenever he looks at anything — like the brachial plexus, like a flower — he says, why does it look like that? How has that come about? What are the rules doing it? It's always why, why, why? Wonderfully penetrating, wonderfully exciting and terrifically frustrating because he doesn't, in a sense, settle upon one thing. He's always looking at things that lie beside it.

The great lady — his drawing of the woman's body showing all the irrigation systems — the bronchial system, the vascular system, the urinary system, the genital system. This is the parallel for the body of the earth set in the body of the woman. It's the microcosm realised. Ultimately it collapses under the weight of its own graphic ambition — it becomes almost indecipherable as he wants to put so much into this single drawing. This is almost an emblematic drawing of Leonardo: he wants total understanding and wants to express it visually in a way which ultimately even he cannot do.
He would have absolutely loved modern computer graphics and visualisation tools — he couldn't have envisaged them but would have loved them.

Leonardo challenged the biblical view of geological time, recognising that fossils on mountains meant those areas were once underwater — evidence of massive, slow change. This was potentially heretical, because the Earth was meant to be God's creation: fixed, static, settled. Leonardo saw instead a dynamic system — the Earth as a living body with thresholds of tolerance, constantly adjusting, constantly in motion.

The body of the Earth in the Codex Leicester: Leonardo thinks about the body of the Earth as an equilateral triangle and the sphere of water — to get a grip upon how this actually works as a physical system. He's the first person who does this diagrammatically, doing the geometry and the statics and the dynamics of the geological problem according to mathematics.

What this means is that the relationship between earth and water is constantly changing, with some small changes and big cataclysms. This is a dynamic view of the Earth — an interacting dynamic unit — which would have been regarded as heretical if published at the time.

Leonardo looks in detail at the body of the Earth and tries to understand how phenomena happen. Mountain springs: he says it's rather like cutting vessels in our temple — you would get blood spouting out. He thinks maybe it's like distillation — vapour condensing on colder stone at the top. He devises experiments to test this. He tests, revises, tests again. He doesn't always resolve everything. Some problems he devotes enormous time and thought to and can't solve, because he doesn't yet have the relevant dynamic laws which were to come along much later.

Some of the most beautiful drawings Leonardo made are simultaneously works of art and works of science. For Leonardo, nature was beautiful in all its aspects, so a work of art is not essentially different from a work of science.

These drawings of water — planks cutting into a stream, creating almost what he called horses' tails — he doesn't just say it looks like that. He says they have the same rule. He's coming up with an explanation for the analogy, or the analogy actually stimulates the explanation. That is probably the way round one should put it: the analogy is the engine of discovery, not merely its illustration.

He called himself a disciple of experience. And this is called a sperientia — an experiment. Is it a real one or is it a thought experiment? I suspect he actually did in his laboratory or his workshop have a tank and actually did this. I don't think you can get results of that complexity just by thinking about it.

He says use millet seed to see what's happening. He said coat the side of the tank with sand so you can see the pattern of the waves. He is building experimental apparatus. He is the disciple of experience.

Leonardo was a very private person. He didn't write about his emotions. Very, very private. Michelangelo wrote passionately about everything, from the spiritual life of his soul to the nastiness of cheese in Rome. But Leonardo — we don't get any of that. So he pours his emotion into the work itself — into the black chalk drawings of the deluge, into the almost unbearable tenderness of certain anatomical studies, into the precision of his observations of water.

He has got a sense of how visual demonstrations can produce what I call the AHA factor. You're thinking: how does this valve operate? How does it work? And then you go — AHA! I can see. And this is one of the more notable qualities of his work: the capacity to make the invisible visible, the complex simple, the abstract sensory.

Nobody demonstrates anatomy like this. It is anatomy as God's engineering. He takes the valve out so it becomes an object in its own right, shows it from above and below, open and shut. Nobody had done this kind of systematic visual argument before.

Leonardo believed that geometrical proportion and mathematical structure are not descriptions of reality but are reality itself. The Vitruvian Man encodes his conviction that the same ratios govern the human body, architecture, and the cosmos simultaneously.
The dodecahedron illustrations for Pacioli's De Divina Proportioni show formal structure and aesthetic perception as inseparable: the mathematical pattern is also the beautiful pattern.

The Golden Horn bridge sketch (1502): a single parabolic arch requiring no fasteners, mortar, or lateral support that resolves all compressive forces through geometry alone. The arch does not merely describe the distribution of forces — it is that distribution, made visible and inhabitable.
Core principle: The arch does not describe the forces — it IS the forces made visible. Aesthetic and analytical perception are the same act. Beauty is correct structure.
The geometrical knot patterns for the Academia Leonardi treat geometry as a form of divine beauty. Structure and beauty were, for Leonardo, identical.

Contemporary application — TongGeometry (2026): treating molecules as geometric objects in 3D space — not symbolic graphs — to predict biological activity. The geometry of the molecule IS its function, exactly as Leonardo held.

Leonardo refused to separate the human body from the earth, biological systems from engineered ones, or animate from inanimate. He recognised that branching patterns in bronchial passages, trees, and river deltas reflect the same universal optimisation principle — and this was not analogy but structural identity.
The theme sheet containing geometry, drapery, trees, hair, and water simultaneously — all subject to the same governing rule.
The movement of hair and the movement of water follow the same rule. Not metaphor: structural isomorphism.
Anatomical studies: The human body is constituted from the same material components as the Earth itself. Soil as flesh, rocks as bones, water as blood — Codex Leicester.
Core principle: Leonardo's theme sheet holds geometry, hair, water, and trees simultaneously because they obey the same law. The connection IS the insight.

Contemporary application — Eiji Nakatsu's Shinkansen 500 nose redesign: the tunnel-shock problem is structurally identical to the kingfisher's air-water transition. Modelling the nose on the bird's bill reduced tunnel boom by 30%, energy consumption by 15%, while increasing speed by 10%.

Leonardo conceived the Earth not as backdrop or resource but as a living, self-regulating body with its own thresholds of tolerance. Geological change was slow and systemic; human responsibility was to understand and respect planetary operations rather than presume dominion over them.

Codex Leicester: the Earth as dynamic rather than static — soil as flesh, rocks as bones, water as blood. Water is the primary agent of transformation, shaping landscape through erosion and sediment transport.
Leonardo challenged the biblical view of geological time, recognising that fossils on mountains meant those areas were once underwater — evidence of massive, slow change.
The hubris of presumed human dominion over nature has been repeatedly challenged by geological and political events that reveal the limits of such presumptions.

Contemporary application — The Planetary Boundaries framework (Rockström et al., 2009): nine Earth-system processes within which human activity must remain. The framework translates Leonardo's organic, systemic conception of the planet into a quantitative instrument — without losing the underlying conviction that the Earth is a single, coupled, self-regulating system with finite tolerance.

Leonardo systematically probed the boundary between the predictable and the indeterminate — not because he lacked knowledge but because unpredictability is a property of certain phenomena, not a failure of understanding. Chaotic systems are not random; they are probabilistic within parametric constraints. Applying deterministic models to chaotic problems is a fundamental error.

Codex Leicester experimental tank drawings — water entering through a bocca, with millet seed and sand tracking wave behaviour — demonstrate systematic probing of the boundary between predictable and indeterminate.
His experimental method anticipated chaos theory (Lorenz, 1963): treating unpredictability not as a failure of knowledge but as a property of the phenomenon itself.
Chaotic systems are not random, nor deterministic in the classical sense. They operate according to probabilistic rules within parametric constraints.

Contemporary application — ECMWF ensemble forecasting (1992): the atmosphere is a chaotic system sensitive to initial conditions, so no single deterministic forecast is honest. Running many forecasts from slightly different initial states and presenting the range of outcomes as a probability distribution is the only epistemically honest approach — exactly the stance Leonardo reaches through observation of turbulent water.

Leonardo held that deep understanding requires the sustained alternation of theoretical abstraction and experiential verification — neither privileged over the other. Pure empiricism cannot generalise; pure rationalism generates elegant but wrong solutions. The dialectic runs in both directions, perpetually.
The water pressure experiment with the leather-sided tank and weighted planks: quantified experiential testing of an abstract hydraulic principle.

The glass model of the aortic valve — later verified by Caltech engineer Morteza Gharib using modern imaging — stands as the most striking example of theory tested through physical experimentation across centuries.
We must respect both the generalisers who produce mathematical insights and the empiricists who test these against the resistance of physical reality.
Systems that privilege theory over observation generate elegant but wrong solutions. Systems that privilege observation over theory cannot generalise. Leonardo's dialectic avoids both failure modes.

Contemporary application — Semmelweis (1847): maternal mortality fell from 16% to below 2% with mandatory handwashing — yet the finding was dismissed because no theoretical framework existed to receive it. The community's instruments of recognition could not see what the evidence was showing. The dialectic failure: experience generating decisive knowledge that theory was not equipped to receive.

Leonardo demonstrated that the deepest acts of understanding — in both art and science — originate in structural intuition: a moment of recognition in which an observer perceives that something significant is occurring in a phenomenon before they can articulate why. Aesthetic and analytical perception are not two faculties but one, applied to the same act of seeing.
The Star of Bethlehem botanical drawing: Leonardo remakes rather than merely records, creating an ideal form that captures the rule behind the appearance.
The Ginevra de' Benci portrait: the curling of hair intuitively follows water dynamics before Leonardo had theorised that connection explicitly.
Both artistic and scientific modes originate in shared intuitive recognition; their divergence lies in methodology and presentation, not in their origin.
The aesthetic is the structural solution, simultaneously and inseparably. A bridge whose beauty is not its structural logic has not yet been solved.

Contemporary application — Calatrava's Alamillo Bridge (1992): a single inclined pylon and thirteen stay-pairs. There is no ornament applied to the structure — the aesthetic IS the structural solution. The structural intuition preceded and generated the formal solution; the rightness of the form was perceptible before the calculations confirmed it.

Forces manageable and beneficial at human scale become destructive when amplified. The planet's tolerance for disturbance does not grow proportionally with the ambition of the engineering. Leonardo's deluge drawings are not fantasies — they are predictions about what happens when human presumption encounters force operating at a scale beyond human control.
Leonardo's deluge drawings: battle tents torn into the sky — a vivid image of nature's indifference to human presumption.
The Scala della Sforzesca di Vigevano: water stepped down a hillside to prevent erosion — a model of working productively with natural force rather than attempting to dominate it.
Forces that sustain life at human scales can prove destructive at larger magnitudes. Failure to respect natural force and act in harmony with natural systems invites catastrophic consequences.
Core principle: Leonardo's deluge drawings are not fantasies. They are predictions. Natural force at scale is indifferent to human intention.

Contemporary application — The Three Gorges Dam: generates 100 TWh annually, provides flood control and navigation. Also: mass upstream sedimentation, disrupted migration patterns, altered hydrology, induced geological instability, displacement of 1.3 million people. The Yangtze's force was not destroyed — it was redirected, delayed, and concentrated in forms the original design did not anticipate.

Leonardo learnt from the failed Arno diversion that water, when properly understood, enables human vision; when coerced, it ultimately defeats human intention. Nothing comes from nothing — thermodynamic limits are not negotiable. Sustainable solutions work with the logic of natural systems, not against their properties.
The Archimedean screw drawings: an early exploration of harnessing rather than fighting water's natural behaviour.
The Arno canal proposal via Prato and Pistoia — following exactly the route of the modern motorway — showed Leonardo working with the landscape's natural logic rather than against it.
Water serves as a subtle ally across scales, yet it cannot be forced against its nature. When properly understood, it enables human vision; when coerced, it ultimately defeats human intentions.
Nothing comes from nothing. Thermodynamic limits are not negotiable.

Contemporary application — The Dutch Room for the River programme (2006–2019): not higher dykes but lower floodplains, removed obstacles, side channels. The conceptual shift from resistance to accommodation — giving water room to move in ways that serve human safety whilst working with the river's own logic. The programme also won a landscape architecture prize: functional and aesthetic were the same thing.

Leonardo recognised that the eye does not passively receive the world but actively constructs it — and that this construction has limits, biases, and blind spots. Perceptual humility is not an obstacle to understanding but its foundation: knowing the limits of what your instruments can see is what makes genuine discovery possible.
The eye does not know the edge of any body. — Manuscript E, c.1508. Leonardo's late loss of faith in optical certainty.
The wax ventricle injection drawings: the transition from theoretical models of vision to direct physical investigation.
The Lumen Cinereum analysis in the Codex Leicester demonstrates simultaneous contrast and the eye's active role in distorting what we perceive.
Core principle: Perception is constructive, not transparent. The history of knowledge is a history of failed predictions revealing the limits of the models that generated them.

Contemporary application — Predictive coding framework (Rao and Ballard, 1999; Friston, 2010): the visual system does not passively receive sensory input but actively generates predictions, comparing them against what actually arrives and updating only in response to discrepancies. What we perceive is largely what the brain expected to perceive.

Beyond what we do not yet know lies a more troubling category: phenomena whose very existence we cannot yet formulate as questions. Leonardo's late works — the Salvator Mundi, the St John the Baptist, the deluge drawings — encode his recognition that mystery and incomprehension are not failures of inquiry but integral features of the human condition.
The Salvator Mundi: the deliberately blurred features and rock crystal sphere represent the boundary between the knowable (the sphere of fixed stars) and the unknowable (what lies beyond).
St John the Baptist, Leonardo's last painting: the finger points toward what cannot be seen or known. Optical uncertainty becomes theological.
The Virgin, Child and St Anne cartoon: the knowing smile of St Anne signals an awareness of secrets that lie beyond rational articulation.

Core principle: The finger points toward what cannot be seen or known. The most consequential discoveries are not answers to existing questions but encounters with what existing questions could not anticipate.

Contemporary application — JWST deep field results (2022): a population of massive, already-mature galaxies 600 million years after the Big Bang — a period in which standard cosmology predicted galaxy formation was still in its earliest stages. The telescope was not built to disprove standard cosmology; it found an unknown unknown: not a question that had been asked and left unanswered, but a configuration of reality the available conceptual framework had not equipped anyone to look for.

The ten models are not a taxonomy of separate intellectual virtues but a description of a single mode of mind. They are isolated here for analytical clarity — but their power is in their simultaneous operation.
The three synthesis exemplars from the paper — Karikó and Weissman's mRNA vaccine platform, the Human Genome Project, and the Montreal Protocol — each instantiated all ten models simultaneously.
The implementation directive: all ten cognitive dispositions must be active on every query. The Questioner always has the last word: every response ends by opening the next, deeper question.

From the paper's conclusion: His integrative approach, refusing the compartmentalisation of knowledge that characterises modern education and professional practice alike, points not towards a nostalgic ideal but towards a cognitive architecture that remains available — and, the evidence suggests, remains necessary. The task is not to replicate Leonardo's particular cognitive trajectory. It is, rather, to recognise in his documented practice a set of cognitive dispositions whose structural properties are identifiable, teachable, and, as the contemporary exemplifications assembled here suggest, generative across domains and eras.
The eye, which is called the window of the soul, is the chief means whereby the understanding may most fully and abundantly appreciate the infinite works of Nature.
Painting is concerned with all the ten attributes of sight, which are: Darkness, Light, Solidity and Colour, Form and Position, Distance and Propinquity, Motion and Rest.
The painter who draws merely by practice and by eye, without any reason, is like a mirror which copies every thing placed in front of it without being conscious of their existence.
The eye does not know the edge of any body. [Manuscript E, c.1508]

All our knowledge has its origin in our perceptions. Science is the observation of things possible, whether present or past; prescience is the knowledge of things which may come to pass, though but slowly. Experience, the interpreter between formative nature and the human race, teaches how that nature acts among mortals; and being constrained by necessity cannot act otherwise than as reason, which is its helm, requires her to act.
There are three classes of people: those who see, those who see when they are shown, those who do not see.
Among the great things which are found among us the existence of Nothing is the greatest.
The natural desire of good men is knowledge.
Iron rusts from disuse, stagnant water loses its purity and in cold weather becomes frozen; even so does inaction sap the vigours of the mind.
Water is the driving force of all nature.

Observe the motion of the surface of the water which resembles that of hair, which has two motions, of which one is caused by the weight of the hair, the other by the direction of the curls; thus the water has eddying motions, one part of which is due to the principal current, the other to the random and reverse motion.
Water, which is beaten on rocks by the sea in its stormy waves, is the most powerful agent of erosion of hard rock.

Among the things relating to water there is one that I must not omit; a wave formed in water when the wind blows over it, and these waves pursue one another, and so long as the wind blows they enlarge themselves, and when the wind ceases they diminish.
The water which rises in mountains is that which falls from the clouds; and it collects together in many rivers and lakes, and rushes down through all the crevices of the mountains to the sea.
When the rock falls into the water, it makes circles; and the circles that form about the rock in water go further from it, the further they go. So does the light in the air.
As the water poured into a still vessel does not rest until it becomes level, so in flowing water every particle strives to become level with the bottom.
Nothing is increased in weight by water except weight. Water added to water does not increase the weight of the water, but each new addition lifts the whole.
In rivers, the water that you touch is the last of what has passed and the first of that which comes; so with present time.
A wave is made in water when the water is moved; and that which moves is not the water but a form running through the water. The water stays in its place.

Water falling in a still pool creates circles from where it falls. At the four sides of these circles, other circles are formed; and these again at their four corners produce other circles, and from their four corners other circles are made; so that one fall produces infinite circles.

The soil of the mountains is constantly being carried down, for rain falling on the mountains carries it to the plain, where it is deposited; and then the waters carry it to the sea, and in this way the mountains are hollowed out, and the plains are filled up.
The human body is constituted from the same material components as the earth itself.

The body of the earth, like the bodies of animals, is interwoven with a network of veins which are all in connection and are formed for the nutrition and vivification of this earth and of its creatures.

I have found that in the human body the veins arise in two modes; the one universal, and that is in the liver, the other particular, and that is in the heart; and that the liver sends its blood through the great vessel to all the members, and the heart sends its blood in pulsations through the arteries.

You will perhaps say that the blood comes from the right ventricle of the heart and not from the left; but do not look at my words, but consider the veins of the liver and of the kidneys and of the testicles.
The heart in itself is not the beginning of life, but it is a vessel made of dense muscle, vivified and nourished by the artery and vein as are the other muscles.

Understand that the heart is the beginning of life; the sun of the microcosm; even as the sun in his turn might be called the heart of the world; for it is the heart that gives life and nourishment to all the body, warming and vivifying the blood which is generated by it.

The man who has intercourse aggressively and uneasily will produce children who are irritable and untrustworthy; but if the intercourse is done with great love and desire on both sides, the child will be of great intellect, witty, lively, and lovable.

From the age of thirty to forty the muscles and nerves grow with the body; from forty to sixty they remain the same; and after that they begin to decrease until they are very similar to those of the young child.

A painter should know the nature of every quality of the things that he proposes to represent. The muscles of the body vary in three ways: first they are equal to the body; second they are larger; third they are smaller.
The eye keeps a third of the qualities of its form; that is to say, the pupil is a third of the iris, the iris a third of the cornea, and the cornea a third of the total sphere of the eye.

Man, rightly called a little world, contains within himself earth, water, air, and fire; for the body of the earth, his bones are rocks; the blood in his veins is water; the expansion and contraction of his breathing is air; the heat of his vital spirits is fire.

A bird is an instrument working according to mathematical law, which instrument it is within the capacity of man to reproduce with all its movements, but not with a corresponding degree of strength, though it is deficient only in the power of maintaining equilibrium. We may therefore say that such an instrument constructed by man is lacking in nothing except the life of the bird, and this life must be supplied from that of man.

The great bird will take its first flight upon the back of the great bird, filling the whole world with amazement and all records with its fame, and it will bring eternal glory to the nest where it was born.

The movement of the birds through the air should be compared to the motion of a boat through water, and the motion of the fish through water and of the air and water themselves: and this comparison will help to understand the motion of birds through the air.

An object offers as much resistance to the air as the air does to the object. You may see that the beating of its wings against the air supports a heavy eagle in the highest and rarest atmosphere, close to the sphere of elemental fire. Also you may see the air in motion over the sea fill the swelling sails and drive heavily laden ships. From these examples and the reasons given, a man with wings large enough and duly connected might learn to overcome the resistance of the air, and by conquering it, succeed in subjugating it and rise above it.
No human investigation can be called real science if it cannot be demonstrated mathematically.
Let no man who is not a mathematician read the elements of my work.
The arm of the balance that has nothing in it is lighter than the arm that has a weight in it; so the arm with greater force raises the lesser weight, and in proportion.
Among the sciences, geometry is the one that the reason most truly comprehends; because it can demonstrate its elements with absolute certainty and truth.
The man who blames the supreme certainty of mathematics feeds on confusion, and will never impose silence on the contradictions of the sophistic sciences, which occasion a perpetual clamour.
Mechanics is the paradise of the mathematical sciences, because by means of it one comes to the fruits of mathematics.
Proportion is found not only in numbers and measures, but also in sounds, weights, times and places, and in whatsoever power it may exist.
Nature has done nothing superfluous; she has done nothing vain; it is the nature of Necessity that determines all.

The arch which is formed by two weaknesses becomes strong. For the two half circles, of which the arch is made, press against one another. And when the arch is complete, the two weaknesses support each other. And the stronger the weight placed on the arch, the more it holds together.

The arch is nothing other than a force originated by two weaknesses, for the arch in buildings is composed of two segments of a circle, and each of these segments being in itself very weak desires to fall, and as the one withstands the downfall of the other, the two weaknesses are converted into a single strength.

Shadow is the absence of light. Shadow is the privation of light and shade is the privation of shadow. The shadow of the same kind is more powerful near its cause. Primitive shadow is that shadow which is inseparable from the body to which it belongs.
The shadow of every opaque body is of the same colour as the body which casts it.
Every opaque body has both light and shadow. And in proportion as the light which lights it is universal, so the shadow which is produced by it will be of even tone.
Where the shadow ends and the light begins, there is neither one nor the other, but something that participates of both.
Darkness is the privation of light; light is the privation of darkness. Both have their limits: for if there be no shadow there is no light, and if there be no light there is no shadow.
Shadow is the means by which bodies display their form. The forms of bodies could not be understood in detail but for shadow.

Every solid body is surrounded by light and shade. When the boundary of shadow and the boundary of light are both adjacent to a line of equal shade, neither the light nor the shade extends beyond this boundary.

O powerful and once-living instrument of formative nature, incapable of availing thyself of thy vast strength as thou didst when thou hadst life, thou art compelled to forsake thy tranquil life to obey a law of God.
Necessity is the mistress and guardian of nature. Necessity is the theme and the inventress, the eternal curb and law of nature.

Gravity and levity are products of nature. They reside in all things. Force is a spiritual power, an invisible energy which is imparted by violence from without to insensible bodies, giving them the semblance of life; this life is of marvellous potency—it constrains all created things and extends its influence throughout every direction; nothing can escape from it, and nothing can endure it long.
The sun gives spirit and life to plants, and the earth nourishes them with moisture.

The painter must study the movements of water, of fire, of wind; how the earth is loosened and how it flows away; how one body dissolves into another; how snow freezes; how the clouds dissipate in rain; how vapour rises; how fire leaps; how bodies rise and fall.
The first object of the painter is to make a flat plane appear as a body in relief and projecting from that plane.

Stones are made from the earth, and the ashes are what was once the marrow of the earth.

What is found in greater quantities in Nature is most universal. What is most universal is most common.
